policy_title: Social Care Workforce Plan and Royal College of Care Workers
stated: Create a social care workforce plan, establish a Royal College of Care Workers to improve recognition and career progression, and introduce a higher Carer’s Minimum Wage (boosting it by £2 an hour) as a starting point for improved pay. This also includes creating clear career pathways, a career ladder to allow flexibility across NHS and social care, and expanding the NHS Digital Staff Passport to include the care sector.

source.quote: Create a social care workforce plan, establish a Royal College of Care Workers to improve recognition and career progression, and introduce a higher Carer’s Minimum Wage. Make careers in social care more attractive and value experienced staff to improve retention by: Creating a new Carer’s Minimum Wage, boosting the minimum wage for care workers by £2 an hour, as a starting point for improved pay across the sector. Creating clear career pathways, linked to recommended pay scales, which put an end to the undervaluing of skills in the sector. Creating a career ladder to allow flexibility to work across the NHS and social care, allowing staff to gain experience in both. Creating a Royal College of Care Workers to represent this skilled workforce. Expanding the NHS Digital Staff Passport to include the care sector.

bearing_set.reason: The £2/hour Carer's Minimum Wage uplift, Royal College recognition, and structured career pathways directly affect pay levels, job quality, and career security for social care workers.

Social care workforce capacity and quality (a direct O8 indicator) would be materially affected by a workforce plan, improved retention via better pay, and clear career progression in the care sector.

Extending the NHS Digital Staff Passport and creating an NHS–social care career ladder directly addresses the workforce interface that drives delayed discharges and NHS capacity; a stronger care workforce reduces pressure on NHS services.

A targeted £2/hour wage floor increase for care workers — concentrated in the bottom income deciles — narrows the income distribution and reduces the Gini coefficient, producing a non-negligible inequality-narrowing effect distinct from the O4 job-quality story.

membership_note: Four fundamentals earn real verdicts: O8 (primary beneficiary — social care access and quality), O4 (direct pay and career quality improvement for a large low-paid workforce), O3 (explicit NHS crossover mechanism via staff passport and career ladder reducing delayed discharges), and O14 (targeted wage uplift for bottom-decile workers narrows income inequality). O12 was considered but the policy does not specify funding, and the fiscal mechanism is insufficiently pinned to score independently.
